own_scenes.desc: Salidos de la San Francisco Mime Troupe y del Artists Liberation Front e inspirados por los Provos, Emmett Grogan, Billy Murcott, Peter Berg y otros tomaron el nombre de los radicales ingleses de Gerrard Winstanley (1649) y publicaron hojas anónimas contra la sociedad americana, contra los comerciantes hip de Haight Street y contra el «trascendentalismo psicodélico» de Leary. Durante el toque de queda de Hunters Point animaron a desafiarlo sin enfrentarse. Hacia el 6 de octubre, el día en que el LSD se hizo ilegal en California (celebrado con el Love Pageant Rally en el Panhandle, con los Grateful Dead y Big Brother), empezaron a dar comida gratis cada día a los jóvenes y fugados que llegaban al Haight: «es gratis porque es tuyo». El Haight ya tenía periódicos, salas, grafismo y sonido propios; Newsweek pensó que podía arrasar el país.

refs.q: The Diggers emerged out of this ferment.
refs.para: The Diggers emerged out of this ferment. Inspired by the Provos, Grogan, his old friend Billy Murcott, Kent Minault, Peter Berg and others began discussions on how they could affect and shape this new community. As Grogan later wrote in his memoir, Ringolevio, ‘They decided to get things real by challenging the street people with the conclusions arrived at during these informal Digger sessions. They mimeographed their thoughts, using a different color paper for each set of leaflets, which soon became known as the Digger Papers.’

refs.q: On Thursday 6 October, LSD became illegal under Californian law.
refs.para: On Thursday 6 October, LSD became illegal under Californian law. The Haight celebrated this fact with an event called the ‘Love Pageant Rally’. The event was trailed in the eighth issue of Mojo Navigator with a new drug-takers’ declaration of independence: ‘We hold these experiences to be self-evident, that all is equal, that the creation endows us with certain inalienable rights, that amongst these are: the freedom of body, the pursuit of joy, and the expansion of consciousness.’

refs.q: Free Food was a shining example of self-help and commitment to the idea of a self-sustaining community
refs.para: Sometime during the week of the Love Pageant Rally, the Diggers began their most fondly remembered action: the distribution of Free Food to the young and needy of the Haight-Ashbury district. The exact date is a matter of some dispute, but it is thought to have taken place on or around 6 October. It began when the Diggers produced a leaflet that advised: ‘BRING A BOWL AND SPOON TO THE PANHANDLE AT ASHBURY STREET 4PM 4PM 4PM 4PM FREE FOOD EVERYDAY FREE FOOD IT’S FREE BECAUSE IT’S YOURS!’ This was an extremely practical solution to the number of young bohemians and runaways who were flocking to the Haight, many of whom had come without any visible means of support. Free Food was a shining example of self-help and commitment to the idea of a self-sustaining community that did things differently to the acquisitive, materialistic American mainstream. The Diggers merely sourced the overflow from markets and food stores; the material was already discarded, and so they turned garbage into sustenance.
